lesson.title: When the Pattern Bends: Understanding Nonlinear Form
lesson.summary: Study nonlinear form through the physics of braking distance, a genuinely quadratic relationship, and learn why linear tools like correlation can badly understate a strong curved pattern.
lesson.body:
A nonlinear form describes a scatterplot whose points follow a curve rather than a straight line: the rate at which the response variable changes is not constant as the explanatory variable increases, so the pattern bends, speeding up, slowing down, or reversing direction as you move across the graph. Where a linear form has a roughly steady rate of change, a nonlinear form has a rate of change that itself changes.

A textbook physical example is the relationship between a car's speed and its braking distance, the distance it travels after the brakes are applied before coming to a full stop. Basic physics explains why this bends: a moving car's kinetic energy is proportional to the square of its speed, and roughly the same braking force has to absorb that energy over the stopping distance. Doubling a car's speed roughly quadruples its kinetic energy, so the braking distance grows much faster than the speed does, producing a curve rather than a straight line.

A simplified, idealized illustration makes the pattern concrete. Suppose braking distance in feet is modeled as 0.05 times speed in miles per hour, squared. At 20 mph, that gives 0.05 times 400, or 20 feet. At 40 mph, double the speed, it gives 0.05 times 1600, or 80 feet, four times as far, not twice as far. At 60 mph, triple the original speed, it gives 0.05 times 3600, or 180 feet, nine times the original distance. Speed only tripled, but stopping distance grew ninefold, and that is exactly the signature of a nonlinear, specifically quadratic, form: equal increases in the explanatory variable produce increasingly larger increases in the response.

This is precisely the situation where the correlation coefficient and a line of best fit can mislead you if applied carelessly. A curve like this braking distance example can be an extremely strong, highly predictable relationship, every single point falls exactly on the curve in the idealized version, yet fitting a straight line through it and computing r would produce a number well below 1, understating how strong and predictable the relationship actually is, because r is only built to detect straight-line patterns. Recognizing the bend by eye, as taught in form of association, has to come before deciding whether r is even the right tool to compute.

Braking distance follows a specific quadratic curve, but nonlinear forms take other shapes as well. Some data grows explosively, like compound interest or the size of a rapidly spreading population, where the response accelerates upward with no leveling off, other data rises quickly at first and then flattens out, like the height of a plant over time as it approaches its mature size. All of these count as nonlinear because none of them changes at a constant rate, even though the specific curves look quite different from one another and from the quadratic braking distance example.

The practical habit to build is simple: before summarizing any scatterplot with a correlation coefficient or fitting it with a straight line, look at the shape of the point cloud first. If the pattern bends consistently in one direction rather than scattering evenly around an imaginary straight line, treat it as nonlinear and be cautious about tools built for linear relationships, since applying them to a curved pattern can distort your conclusions about how strong the relationship really is.
